top_strength: Joel's estimate is the strongest thing here, because he built it out of the actual job instead of a generic bedroom count. He narrated the variables straight into the number: 'We're loading up on the fifth floor potentially a long walk, just depends and then thirty minute drive and unloading all the bedroom, all the furniture, and the second floor let's just save the mover to take about four hours. We're looking into the total cost of $955 and then five hours is $1,175.' That is exactly the estimate-accuracy behavior the rubric is trying to build. He was also genuinely proactive on the logistics the customer could not have known to raise - she was confused about the parking garage, and rather than take her word for it he ruled it out with a real constraint ('we wouldn't be able to park the truck or get the truck through the parking garage or trucks about thirteen feet in height') and explained the workaround. His clock explanation was complete and clean, and the whole intake ran in about seven minutes.
coaching_note: He skipped the entire differentiator block - No Worries Damage Coverage, Meet Your Mover, and the On-Time Guarantee all went unsaid - and that is 6 of the 8 points lost in Section 3 plus the insurance bonus. Compare it to his own Houston call twelve minutes earlier, where he delivered all three well; here the whole value pitch collapsed into 'We don't have any additional charges for your move, it's just the hourly rate.' That matters more than usual on this call: this was a referral ('A friend of mine moved her daughter into an apartment using you guys'), which is the easiest audience for the trust pitch, and at $220/hr with nothing else said, price is the only thing she has to compare. The second thing to fix is cheaper and faster - she apologized twice for not knowing details and said 'I'm not sure. Sorry, I'm not really helpful,' and he moved straight to the next question. One line of reassurance there costs nothing and is the difference between a transaction and a relationship. Note for context: the call drops mid-sentence after the quote ('Can you hear me okay?'), so the booking section never got a chance - but the differentiators normally come before the estimate and were already skipped by then.
phone_presence_notes: Efficient and competent but almost entirely transactional - her name is used once while reading back an email address, there are no affirmations or empathy markers anywhere in seven minutes, and her two apologies for not knowing details were met with the next question rather than any reassurance.

Hello?' / 'Can you hear me okay?'), so it is unclear how much of the low-warmth read is the rep and how much is a degrading connection.
